mcqs.question: Why did browsers historically open ~6 parallel TCP connections per host under HTTP/1.1?
options: To work around per-connection head-of-line blocking — since only one request per connection can be in flight until its response fully returns
Because each new connection lets the browser skip repeating the TLS handshake for that origin
To spread requests across multiple IP addresses for faster DNS resolution
Because HTTP/1.1 caps each connection to a fixed number of bytes total
mcqs.explanation: Parallel connections exist purely to route around per-connection HOL blocking. Every one of those connections still repeats its own TLS handshake — that's part of the overhead problem, not something avoided. DNS resolution speed and byte caps aren't real HTTP/1.1 constraints.

mcqs.question: In HTTP/2, how does the receiving end know which bytes on the wire belong to which in-flight request?
options: Each request gets a dedicated TCP connection, so there's no ambiguity
Each frame carries a stream ID, so frames from different requests can be interleaved and reassembled by ID
Frames are timestamped, and the receiver reorders them by arrival time
HTTP/2 sends one request fully before starting the next, same as HTTP/1.1
mcqs.explanation: Stream IDs on every frame are the actual mechanism. Dedicated connections per request describes HTTP/1.1's workaround, not HTTP/2. Frames aren't reassembled by timestamp, and HTTP/2's entire point is not serializing requests the way HTTP/1.1 does.

mcqs.question: What specifically does HPACK save that gzip/deflate body compression wouldn't?
options: The number of TCP connections needed per origin
The size of the response body on every request
Repeated header bytes across requests, via a shared static/dynamic table so a header seen before is sent as a small index instead of full text
The time needed to parse binary frames
mcqs.explanation: HPACK specifically targets header repetition across requests — a separate problem from body compression, which gzip/deflate already handle. It doesn't change connection counts or frame-parsing time.

mcqs.question: Why did browsers largely drop support for HTTP/2 server push?
options: Browsers found push slowed down TLS handshakes
Push required a new binary frame type that turned out to be technically impossible to implement
Push was replaced because HTTP/1.1 already supported the same feature natively
Servers had no reliable way to know what the client already had cached, so push often wasted bandwidth re-sending cached resources
mcqs.explanation: The real-world failure mode was wasted bandwidth from pushing already-cached resources, with no cache-awareness signal available to the server. Push was fully implementable (it shipped for years) and HTTP/1.1 never had an equivalent feature.

mcqs.question: A single HTTP/2 connection experiences one dropped TCP segment. What's the effect on the other multiplexed streams sharing that connection?
options: All streams on that connection stall until the lost segment is retransmitted and delivered in order, because TCP guarantees in-order byte delivery
No effect — HTTP/2 streams are fully independent even at the TCP layer
Only the stream that owned the lost segment is affected; others proceed unaffected
The connection immediately closes and a new one is opened automatically
mcqs.explanation: This is transport-layer head-of-line blocking: TCP's in-order delivery guarantee means every multiplexed stream on that connection stalls, not just the one that lost data. HTTP/2 streams are independent at the HTTP layer, not the TCP layer beneath it.
